Election Day: Tuesday, Nov. 3

Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, 6:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. A voter in line by 7:00 p.m. can vote. The 51 vote centers, including Truman College, keep the same hours.

Your polling place: Goudy School, 5120 N. Winthrop Ave., Chicago, IL.

The Board's list of Oct. 27 says that the list can change. Check your polling place and sample ballot · Polling place list

Early voting, through Nov. 2

Truman College (46th Ward early voting site), 1145 W. Wilson Ave., Chicago, IL.

Thu., Oct. 29 and Fri., Oct. 30: 9:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Sat., Oct. 31: 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Sun., Nov. 1: 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Mon., Nov. 2: 9:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. On Election Day it serves as a vote center, 6:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. Any Chicago voter can use any early voting site.

Early voting sites and hours

Vote by mail

The deadline to apply for a mail ballot is 5:00 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Return the ballot only in its signed and sealed Ballot Return Envelope. A mailed envelope counts if its postmark is on or before Election Day and it arrives within 14 days after. A drop box at any early voting site or Election Day vote center also works. So does the Board office at 69 W. Washington St., Suite 600. Precinct polling places take no mail ballots. A voter can also surrender an unused mail ballot and vote in person.

Drop boxes near you:

  • Truman College (46th Ward), 1145 W. Wilson Ave.
  • Broadway Armory (48th Ward), 5917 N. Broadway St.
  • Welles Park (47th Ward), 2333 W. Sunnyside Ave.
  • Merlo Library (44th Ward), 644 W. Belmont Ave.

Vote by mail rules · All drop boxes

Register or update your address

Online registration closed Oct. 18, 2026. Same-day registration runs at every early voting site through Nov. 2. On Election Day, register at your home precinct polling place or any of the 51 vote centers. Bring two forms of ID, and one must show your current address. Accepted IDs include a driver's license or state ID, passport, lease, utility bill, bank statement, pay stub, or government mail.

Registration rules · ID rules

Notes in the booth

Yes. The Chicago Board of Elections' Voters' Bill of Rights says every voter has the right to use endorsements, sample ballots, or notes while voting.

Election Day voting page

Not on this ballot: Mayor

Chicago elects its Mayor, City Clerk, and City Treasurer on Tuesday, Feb. 23, 2027. A runoff follows on April 6, 2027, if no candidate gets a majority.

Federal and state offices 8 races, all contested

United States Senator

3 candidatesVote for 1Open seat

One of Illinois' two members of the 100-seat U.S. Senate, for a six-year term. Senators vote on federal laws and confirm federal judges and cabinet members.

Open seat: Democrat Dick Durbin retires. Stratton and Tracy clashed over the cost of living, tariffs, immigration enforcement, and the minimum wage. Three forecasters rate the race Solid or Safe Democratic, per Ballotpedia.

1 Don Tracy RepublicanSenior counsel, Brown, Hay & Stephens law firm

Don Tracy is a Springfield attorney and outside general counsel to Dot Foods, a food distributor that his parents founded. He chaired the Illinois Gaming Board and led the Illinois Republican Party from 2021 to 2024. He quit the party post amid party infighting. He never held elected office and lost a 2010 Republican primary for lieutenant governor.

Priorities and endorsements · Links (3) · Not verified (2)
Stated priorities and endorsements
  • Lower the cost of living: housing, groceries, utilities, and health care (campaign site).
  • Voter ID and proof of citizenship to register to vote, plus tighter mail-in voting rules.
  • Opposes a $25 federal minimum wage and calls it a 'death sentence for small businesses.'
  • Sees tariffs as a negotiating tool. He called the federal 'Operation Midway Blitz' immigration crackdown 'ugly and chaotic.'
  • Says his support for President Trump 'depends on the policy.' He did not seek Trump's endorsement but accepts one.

  • The years of his Illinois Gaming Board chairmanship (2015 to 2019) come from a search summary only.
2 Juliana Stratton DemocraticLieutenant Governor of Illinois

Juliana Stratton became lieutenant governor in 2019 as JB Pritzker's running mate. Before that, she served in the Illinois House and worked as a lawyer and mediator. She beat U.S. Representatives Raja Krishnamoorthi and Robin Kelly in the March primary, with millions of dollars in support from Pritzker. If she wins, she becomes Illinois' fourth Black U.S. senator.

In the news
  • Barack Obama endorses Juliana Stratton for Senate in slew of midterm picks Chicago Sun-Times · Oct. 12, 2026Former President Barack Obama endorsed Stratton.
Priorities and endorsements · Links (4) · Not verified (2)
Stated priorities and endorsements
  • Abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and create a path to citizenship, including for Dreamers.
  • A $25 federal minimum wage and a tax on millionaires.
  • Opposes Trump's trade war. She wants tariff refunds paid to Illinois residents, not large corporations.
  • Opposes cuts to health care and food aid, and wants wider health care access.
  • Backs impeaching Trump. In the primary, she alone said she opposes Chuck Schumer as Senate Democratic leader.

Governor & Lieutenant Governor

3 candidatesVote for 1

The governor runs the state's executive branch, proposes the state budget, and signs or vetoes bills. Voters pick the governor and lieutenant governor as one ticket, for a four-year term.

Democrat JB Pritzker seeks a third term in a rematch with Republican Darren Bailey, whom he beat by nearly 13 points in 2022. A Public Policy Polling survey from September 30 to October 1 showed Pritzker at 54%, Bailey 34%, and Corbett 6%. Main issues include property taxes, cash bail, immigration enforcement, the Chicago Bears stadium, and data centers.

4 Darren Bailey & Aaron B. Del Mar RepublicanFarmer; former state legislator

Darren Bailey is a Xenia farmer and a former state lawmaker from southern Illinois. He and his wife founded Full Armor Christian Academy, a private school. He lost to Pritzker in 2022 and won the March 2026 Republican primary by 24 points. Running mate Aaron B. Del Mar chairs the Cook County Republican Party and is Palatine Township highway commissioner. Del Mar ran for lieutenant governor in 2022.

In the news
  • President Trump endorses Darren Bailey in Illinois governor race — 'Pritzker's a disaster' Chicago Sun-Times · Sept. 14, 2026President Trump endorsed Bailey. Trump lost Illinois by 11 points in 2024.
  • Bailey trying to stay on message as attacks from Pritzker mount Capitol News Illinois (via NPR Illinois) · Oct. 7, 2026Pritzker ads cite a textbook at Bailey's school on dinosaurs and humans. Bailey walked back his 2022 'hellhole' remark about Chicago.
Priorities and endorsements · Links (2) · Not verified (2)
Stated priorities and endorsements
  • Cap property tax bills at 1%, paid for by a shift in state spending.
  • Repeal the SAFE-T Act (Safety, Accountability, Fairness and Equity-Today Act), the law that ended cash bail.
  • Repeal the 2021 Climate and Equitable Jobs Act, which many Republicans blame for rising energy prices.
  • Create an 'Illinois DOGE' (Department of Government Efficiency) panel, led by Del Mar, to cut waste.
  • Personally opposes abortion, but says he will not try to undo Illinois abortion laws.

JB Pritzker became governor in 2019 and now seeks a third term. A win makes him the first governor since Republican Jim Thompson to win a third term. He funds his own campaign: $90.5 million this cycle, from a fortune that Forbes puts at $4.2 billion. Running mate Christian Mitchell is a former Chicago state representative and was deputy governor in Pritzker's first term. Mitchell's campaign bio also lists Illinois Air National Guard service.

Attorney General

2 candidatesVote for 1

The attorney general is the state's top lawyer. The office sues and defends for the state and its residents, including consumer protection cases. The term lasts four years.

Kwame Raoul is the incumbent and seeks a third term. The race centers on his lawsuits against the federal government and on crime and corruption. Lawmakers cut his office budget by $10 million this year.

7 Robert W. Fioretti RepublicanAttorney; former Chicago alderman

Bob Fioretti is a trained civil rights attorney and a former Democrat who now runs as a Republican. He served as alderman of Chicago's 2nd Ward from 2007 to 2015. Earlier he worked as an assistant Illinois attorney general and in the city's law department. He lost two races for mayor and races for Cook County Board president and Cook County state's attorney.

  • Stop press releases about lawsuits that Raoul does not lead; he agrees with only three of Raoul's suits against the Trump administration (Capitol News Illinois).
  • "Shake things up" in the office, citing unnamed corruption and crime (Chicago Sun-Times).

Comptroller

2 candidatesVote for 1Open seat

The comptroller is the state's chief fiscal officer. The office pays the state's bills, records every transaction, and reviews spending and contracts. It also regulates cemeteries and crematories. The term lasts four years.

Open seat. Comptroller Susana Mendoza, a Democrat in office since late 2016, did not seek reelection; she runs for Chicago mayor instead. Issues include tracking state spending, pension debt, and funeral industry oversight.

He served eight years on the Rend Lake Community College board and placed second in a 2024 Republican primary for circuit judge. He raised just under $80,000 and runs no paid ads.

Treasurer

2 candidatesVote for 1

The treasurer is the state's chief investment and banking officer. The office invests about $60 billion for the state and local governments. It also returns unclaimed property and runs college savings programs. The term lasts four years.

Michael W. Frerichs is the incumbent and seeks a fourth term. No Republican filed for the March primary. Max Solomon won the Republican line with more than 60,000 write-in votes (Capitol News Illinois).

U.S. Representative, 9th District

2 candidatesVote for 1Open seat

One of 435 members of the U.S. House of Representatives, for a two-year term. Members vote on federal laws and the federal budget.

Open seat: Democrat Jan Schakowsky retires, and the seat is open for the first time in 26 years. The district covers parts of Chicago's North Side and nearby suburbs, including Evanston and Skokie. We found no debate between the two nominees.

John Elleson is a minister at Lakewood Chapel and lives in Arlington Heights. He says he served as a Chicago-area pastor for 40 years, and he holds a college degree in pastoral ministries. He never held public office and lost to Schakowsky in 2018, 73.5% to 26.5%. He won the March 2026 Republican primary with about 49% of the vote.

Judge of the Appellate Court (Vacancy of Hoffman)

UnopposedVote for 1 102 Judith C. Rice DemocraticPresiding judge, Domestic Violence Division, Circuit Court of Cook County

All 14 bar groups positive

The Illinois Appellate Court reviews circuit court decisions when a party appeals. The First District covers Cook County and meets in Chicago. Justices serve 10-year terms, then face yes-or-no retention votes.

Justice Thomas E. Hoffman held this seat; the ballot names each open seat after its last holder. Judith C. Rice is the only candidate. She is the same Judith C. Rice who appears later on this ballot for retention as a circuit judge. Injustice Watch reports that she will resign her circuit seat if she wins this appellate seat.

Voters elected Rice a Cook County circuit judge in 2014, and she became presiding judge of the Domestic Violence Division in 2021. Before that, she worked as a BMO Harris Bank executive, Chicago City Treasurer (2000-2006), and a city department head under Mayor Richard M. Daley. Injustice Watch reports that advocates for domestic violence survivors regard her highly for her management of the domestic violence courthouse.

Chicago Board of Education 2 races, all contested

President of the Chicago Board of Education

4 candidatesVote for 1

The president runs meetings and helps set the agenda for the 21-member board that oversees Chicago Public Schools (CPS). The board approves the budget, hires the schools chief, can raise property taxes, and serves without pay; the president's term lasts four years.

In 2026, for the first time, voters elect all 21 seats: 20 subdistrict members and a citywide president. In 2024 voters chose 10 members, and the mayor appointed the other 11; the new board takes office in January 2027. CPS faced a $732.5 million deficit for 2026-27. In July 2026 the board voted 11-7 for a budget that cancelled over 1,000 layoffs and counted on $150 million in uncommitted state money. Mayor Brandon Johnson, a former union official and close ally of the Chicago Teachers Union (CTU), pushed CPS in 2024 to take a high-interest loan. His board appointees resigned in October 2024, and his new appointees fired schools chief Pedro Martinez that December. In August 2025 the board again refused the mayor's push for a high-cost loan. Groups opposed to the CTU outraised the union about 5 to 1, and total election spending topped $9 million by Oct. 21. Sendhil Revuluri ended his campaign on Sept. 30, 2026, but his name stays on the ballot.

121 Victor P. Henderson NonpartisanAttorney; founder of the law firm Henderson Parks

Henderson, 65, of Beverly, is a defense attorney and former certified public accountant who once led the Chicago Bar Association. He sits on the board of Urban Prep charter schools, and his four children attended CPS schools. He is the only candidate without education work experience. He lent his campaign $500,000, which lifted donation limits for all candidates, and reported just over $300,000 on hand on Sept. 30.

Member of the Chicago Board of Education, Subdistrict 2B

3 candidatesVote for 1

The Subdistrict 2B member holds one of 21 seats on the board that oversees Chicago Public Schools (CPS). Members approve the budget, hire the schools chief, can raise property taxes, and serve without pay.

In 2026, for the first time, voters elect all 21 board seats. Subdistrict 2B covers Lincoln Square, Edgewater, Albany Park, Uptown, and North Park, with 18 schools and 15,178 students. This year, seats now held by mayoral appointees carry a two-year term. Incumbent Debby Pope, a former Chicago Teachers Union (CTU) staffer, joined the board in 2024 as Mayor Brandon Johnson's appointee. She faces Kyna Lenhof, a former special education teacher. Daniel Basco ended his campaign on Oct. 11 and endorsed Lenhof, but his name stays on the ballot. The CTU backs Pope; Common Ground Collective, a political action committee (PAC) that billionaire Michael Sacks largely funds, backs Lenhof. CPS faced a $732.5 million deficit. Common Ground ran an ad attacking Pope's vote for a budget that counted on $150 million in uncommitted state money.

131 Deborah "Debby" Pope NonpartisanIncumbentChicago Board of Education member, Subdistrict 2B (appointed 2024)

Pope, 74, of Edgewater/West Andersonville, taught bilingual social studies in CPS high schools for close to 20 years, including Juárez and Gage Park. After retiring, she worked on the CTU staff for just over a decade. Mayor Johnson appointed her to the board in 2024, after his first appointees resigned. She raised $13,006 by Sept. 16; the CTU's political arm was her top donor.

  • Wants multiyear budgets and published school-level impacts before votes, with special education, bilingual staff, counselors, and nurses cut last.
  • Wants guardrails on artificial intelligence (AI) to protect student data and privacy.
  • Supports closures only with years of notice and community consent; opposes new charters after a 20% enrollment drop in a decade.
  • Refused money from the union and from charter advocates; calls himself "beholden to neither side."

Judges up for retention 60 Yes-or-No votes

Judges in a retention race face no opponent. Voters answer Yes or No on whether each judge stays for another term. A judge keeps the seat only with Yes votes from at least 60% (three-fifths) of the voters who answer that judge's question. A retained circuit judge serves six more years, and a retained appellate judge serves ten more years.

6 judges got a negative rating from at least one bar group. 10 more have a news note and no negative rating. The research found neither for the other 44.

Ballot questions 8

An advisory question changes no law. It tells officials what voters want. A binding question takes effect if it passes.

The Cook County Millionaire Amendment for Property Tax Relief and Education

AdvisoryCook County voters

This is an advisory question. It asks voters if they want Illinois to add a 3% income tax surcharge on millionaires. Half the money goes to property tax relief and half to public schools. The vote changes no law; the plan needs a change to the state constitution.

A Yes vote

You tell state leaders that you support the 3% millionaire surcharge, split between property tax relief and schools.

A No vote

You tell state leaders that you oppose the 3% millionaire surcharge.

Ballot text · Background · For and against · News (3) · Official pages · Not verified (3)
Ballot text
"Shall Illinois adopt the Millionaire Amendment for Property Tax Relief and Education, which would enact a 3% income tax surcharge only on millionaires and use 50% of this new revenue to provide property tax relief for residential and commercial taxpayers and 50% to improve state funding for public education?"
Background

The question mirrors House Joint Resolution Constitutional Amendment 21 (HJRCA0021), filed in the Illinois House in October 2025. The surcharge applies only to the part of income above $1 million, with an estimated yield of about $4 billion a year. A binding statewide millionaires tax plan failed in the legislature in spring 2026.

On the ballot by: Cook County Board of Commissioners, by a unanimous vote in July 2026, on a resolution from Commissioner Donna Miller.

Supporters
  • Commissioner Donna Miller (6th District), sponsor of the resolution
  • Commissioner Josina Morita (13th District)
  • Former Gov. Pat Quinn backed a similar question for Chicago's ballot
Opponents and critics
  • Illinois Policy, a research and advocacy group: its Oct. 14 article argues against the tax and the constitutional change it needs
In the news
  • Cook County votes to give opinion on statewide millionaire tax The Record (from the Evanston RoundTable) · July 26, 2026Covers the County Board vote, the sponsor, and the $4 billion revenue estimate.
  • Cook County to vote on non-binding 'millionaires tax' question Illinois Policy · Oct. 14, 2026The main argument against the tax that this research found; written by an advocacy group.
  • Election 2026: Your guide to Chicago-area ballot questions, referenda Fox 32 Chicago · Oct. 14, 2026One guide to every question on this ballot except the mental health questions.
Official and reference pages
  • Official candidate and referenda list, Chicago Board of Elections (Oct. 27, 2026)
  • Specimen ballot, Chicago Board of Elections
Not verified (3)
  • Sources disagree on the County Board file number (one gives 26-1964). This research did not confirm the meeting date of the vote.
  • The $4 billion estimate comes from the news report. This research found no official fiscal note.
  • This research found no named group campaigning for a yes vote besides the commissioners.

Restart Chicago Gunshot Detection

AdvisoryCity of Chicago voters

This is an advisory question. It asks if voters want Chicago to bring back technology that detects gunshots and alerts police and other first responders. The result does not require the city to act.

A Yes vote

You tell city leaders that you want gunshot detection technology back in use.

A No vote

You tell city leaders that you do not want gunshot detection technology back.

Ballot text · Background · For and against · News (2) · Official pages · Not verified (2)
Ballot text
"Should the City of Chicago restart the use of gunshot detection technology that informs first responders when gunshots are detected?"
Background

Mayor Brandon Johnson turned off the city's ShotSpotter system in September 2024, saying it was ineffective. In May 2024 the City Council voted 34-14 to require a council vote before ShotSpotter left any ward. Fox 32 reported in October 2026 that the city had no approved replacement in use.

On the ballot by: Chicago City Council, July 2026, from a resolution by Ald. Marty Quinn (13th Ward).

Supporters
  • Ald. Marty Quinn (13th Ward), lead sponsor
  • Co-sponsors: Alds. Brian Hopkins (2nd), Monique Scott (24th), Peter Chico (10th), Derrick Curtis (18th), Brendan Reilly (42nd), and Matt O'Shea (19th)
Opponents and critics
  • None named in the sources found.
In the news
  • Chicago Voters Won't Weigh Whether to Tax Millionaires — But Will Be Asked About ShotSpotter, Festivals WTTW · July 15, 2026Explains the council fight over which three questions reached the ballot.
  • City Council Votes 34-14 to Endorse Effort to Overturn Mayor Brandon Johnson's Decision to Scrap ShotSpotter WTTW · May 22, 2024The 2024 dispute between the mayor and the council over ending ShotSpotter.
Official and reference pages
  • City Council resolution R2026-0025451 (Councilmatic)
  • Official candidate and referenda list, Chicago Board of Elections (Oct. 27, 2026)
Not verified (2)
  • This research found no named person or group campaigning against this question.
  • Councilmatic still lists the resolution as referred. This research did not see the final council action. WTTW and The Daily Line confirm it is on the ballot.

Permanent Chicago Festival Space

AdvisoryCity of Chicago voters

This is an advisory question. It asks if voters want Chicago to build a permanent site for large festivals and outdoor events. It names no site, no cost, and no owner or operator.

A Yes vote

You tell city leaders that you want a permanent site for large festivals and events.

A No vote

You tell city leaders that you do not want such a site.

Ballot text · Background · For and against · News (2) · Official pages · Not verified (2)
Ballot text
"Should Chicago develop a permanent festival and outdoor event space for large-scale events?"
Background

Lollapalooza and the Sueños festival closed much of Grant Park for several months in recent summers. Some Douglass Park neighbors push to move Riot Fest out of that park. The sponsor named no location for a new site.

On the ballot by: Chicago City Council, July 2026, from a resolution by Ald. Nicole Lee (11th Ward).

Supporters
  • Ald. Nicole Lee (11th Ward), lead sponsor
  • Co-sponsors: Alds. Ronnie Mosley (21st), Brian Hopkins (2nd), Felix Cardona Jr. (31st), Bennett Lawson (44th), and Matt O'Shea (19th)
  • Sara Heymann, organizer of the effort to move Riot Fest out of Douglass Park, told WBEZ she plans to vote yes
Opponents and critics
  • None named in the sources found.

Official and reference pages

Chicago Cost Recovery from Midway Blitz

AdvisoryCity of Chicago voters

This is an advisory question. It asks if voters want Chicago to seek money from the federal government for costs of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) operations. The costs it lists are lost tax revenue, public safety response, and services to affected families. The vote itself starts no lawsuit or claim.

A Yes vote

You tell city leaders that you want the city to seek repayment from the federal government for these costs.

A No vote

You tell city leaders that you do not want the city to seek this repayment.

Ballot text · Background · For and against · News (3) · Official pages · Not verified (2)
Ballot text
"Shall the City of Chicago pursue all lawful means to recover financial compensation from the federal government for the costs and economic harm caused by the Donald Trump administration's violent, militarized ICE operations, including the Midway Blitz operation led by Greg Bovino, to recover lost tax revenue, public safety response costs, and services provided to residents and families affected by those operations?"
Background

Operation Midway Blitz was a federal immigration enforcement operation in Chicago and its suburbs, led by Border Patrol official Gregory Bovino. It began in September 2025. The news reports found give no dollar figure for Chicago's costs.

On the ballot by: Chicago City Council, July 22, 2026, by a 46-1 vote, on a resolution from Mayor Brandon Johnson.

Supporters
  • Mayor Brandon Johnson, author of the resolution
  • 46 alderpersons voted yes on July 22, 2026
Opponents and critics
  • Ald. Anthony Napolitano (41st Ward), the only no vote on July 22, 2026
  • On July 15, Napolitano and Ald. Anthony Beale (9th Ward) used a procedural move to delay the vote, per WTTW
In the news
  • Chicago referendum will ask if city should seek compensation after 'Midway Blitz' NBC Chicago · July 22, 2026Covers the council vote and the mayor's reasons.
  • 'Operation Midway Blitz' in Chicago area sparked shootings, tear gas, protests in 2025 ABC7 ChicagoBackground on the 2025 operation itself.
  • Chicago Voters Won't Weigh Whether to Tax Millionaires — But Will Be Asked About ShotSpotter, Festivals WTTW · July 15, 2026Describes the July 15 delay of this question by two alderpersons.
Official and reference pages
  • City Council resolution R2026-0026834 and roll call (Councilmatic)
  • Official candidate and referenda list, Chicago Board of Elections (Oct. 27, 2026)
Not verified (2)
  • The September 2025 start date comes from an ABC7 search result summary. This research did not open the ABC7 page, and its date is unknown.
  • This research found no estimate of Chicago's costs from the operation.

ADVISORY QUESTION REGARDING MILLIONAIRES SURCHARGE

AdvisoryVoters of Chicago Public Schools (CPS) District 299

This is an advisory question from the Chicago Board of Education. It asks if voters want Illinois to spend money from a tax surcharge on millionaires on public schools. It sets no rate and changes no law.

A Yes vote

You tell state leaders that you want millionaire surcharge money to go to public schools.

A No vote

You tell state leaders that you do not support this use of a millionaire surcharge.

Ballot text · Background · For and against · News (1) · Official pages · Not verified (1)
Ballot text
"Shall Illinois use revenue from a surcharge on millionaires to increase funding to public schools?"
Background

CPS faces a budget deficit. The board balanced its budget by counting on $150 million in extra state money that lawmakers did not yet approve. A binding millionaires tax plan failed in the legislature in spring 2026.

On the ballot by: Chicago Board of Education, by a vote on Aug. 13, 2026.

Supporters
  • Board President Sean Harden
  • Board Vice President Angel Velez
  • Mayor Brandon Johnson favors a millionaires tax, per Chalkbeat
Opponents and critics
  • Board member Jennifer Custer, the only no vote; she called the questions "window dressing to a larger problem"
  • Critic: the Civic Federation, a budget research group, said such referendums make little headway on CPS money problems
In the news
  • A divided Chicago school board adds referendums on new revenue to November ballot Chalkbeat Chicago · Aug. 13, 2026Covers the board vote, the arguments on both sides, and the CPS budget gap.
Official and reference pages
  • Official candidate and referenda list, Chicago Board of Elections (Oct. 27, 2026)
Not verified (1)
  • Chalkbeat gives no exact vote tally; it names Custer as the only no vote on both CPS questions.

ADVISORY QUESTION REGARDING CHICAGO LAND OWNERS

AdvisoryVoters of Chicago Public Schools (CPS) District 299

This is an advisory question from the Chicago Board of Education. It asks if voters want Chicago to charge owners of long-vacant or undeveloped commercial or investment property a new yearly fee. The fee money goes to CPS. It sets no amount and changes no law.

A Yes vote

You tell city leaders that you support a yearly charge on long-vacant commercial or investment property to help fund CPS.

A No vote

You tell city leaders that you oppose this charge.

Ballot text · Background · For and against · News (1) · Official pages · Not verified (1)
Ballot text
"Should the City of Chicago require owners of long-term vacant or undeveloped commercial or investment properties to pay an additional annual charge that would support Chicago Public Schools?"
Background

Board member Cydney Wallace introduced this question. She tied vacant lots to safety for students on their way to school. CPS faces a budget deficit and counts on state money that lawmakers did not yet approve.

On the ballot by: Chicago Board of Education, by a vote on Aug. 13, 2026.

Supporters
  • Board member Cydney Wallace, who introduced the question
  • Board President Sean Harden and Vice President Angel Velez spoke for the CPS questions
Opponents and critics
  • Board member Jennifer Custer, the only no vote
  • Critic: the Civic Federation, a budget research group, said such referendums make little headway on CPS money problems
In the news
  • A divided Chicago school board adds referendums on new revenue to November ballot Chalkbeat Chicago · Aug. 13, 2026Covers the board vote, the arguments on both sides, and the CPS budget gap.
Official and reference pages

Mid-Northside Expanded Mental Health Services

BindingVoters of the proposed Mid-Northside Expanded Mental Health Services Program Area (Edgewater, Lincoln Square, and Uptown)

This binding question creates a local mental health program for Edgewater, Lincoln Square, and Uptown if it passes. The program offers free mental health services to any resident in need. A new property tax of up to 0.025% of each property's taxable value pays for it. A nine-member local commission oversees the money.

A Yes vote

You vote to create the program and the property tax that funds it.

A No vote

You vote against creating the program and its property tax.

Ballot text · Background · For and against · Official pages · Not verified (6)
Ballot text
"Shall there be established, to serve the territory commonly described on this ballot or notice of this question, a Mid-Northside Expanded Mental Health Services Program, to provide direct free mental health services for any resident of the territory who needs assistance in overcoming or coping with mental or emotional disorders, where such program will be funded through an increase of not more than .025% of the equalized assessed valuation of all properties within the boundaries of the territory?"
Background

A state law, the Community Expanded Mental Health Services Act, lets neighborhoods create these programs by petition and referendum. Eight such program areas already exist in Chicago. Residents signed petitions with more than 11,000 signatures to put this question on the ballot.

On the ballot by: Petition of area residents. A Community Action Team of local residents gathered the signatures. The Coalition to Save Our Mental Health Centers submitted them to the Chicago Board of Elections.

Supporters
  • Coalition to Save Our Mental Health Centers (campaigns for a yes vote)
  • The Community Action Team of local residents that gathered the signatures
Opponents and critics
  • None named in the sources found.
Official and reference pages
  • Official candidate and referenda list, Chicago Board of Elections (Oct. 27, 2026)
  • Specimen ballot with the English and Spanish text, Chicago Board of Elections
  • State law: Community Expanded Mental Health Services Act, section 15 (405 ILCS 22/15)
  • Campaign toolkit with service-area map (Coalition to Save Our Mental Health Centers)
  • Current and upcoming program areas (Coalition to Save Our Mental Health Centers)
Not verified (6)
  • This research did not find the official legal description of the territory. The ballot and the specimen ballot do not print it.
  • The boundary used here is the campaign's map, which shows the whole Edgewater, Lincoln Square, and Uptown community areas.
  • Precinct 46-23 lies wholly inside the Uptown community area (City of Chicago boundary data), so it is inside the area on the campaign's map.
  • The nine-member commission and the eight existing program areas come from the campaign's own materials.
  • This research found no news coverage of this 2026 question in Block Club Chicago, WBEZ, the Sun-Times, or the Tribune.
  • This research found no named opponent.

2027 Property Tax Extension - Mid-Northside Expanded Mental Health Services

BindingVoters of the proposed Mid-Northside Expanded Mental Health Services Program Area (Edgewater, Lincoln Square, and Uptown)

This binding question sets a tax limit for the program in the previous question. It lets the program collect up to $1,300,000 in property tax for the 2027 levy year. The ballot ties the request to the state Property Tax Extension Limitation Law.

A Yes vote

You approve a property tax levy of up to $1.3 million for the program in the 2027 levy year.

A No vote

You reject that $1.3 million levy for the 2027 levy year.

Ballot text · Background · For and against · Official pages · Not verified (3)
Ballot text
"Under the Property Tax Extension Limitation Law, may an aggregate extension not to exceed $1,300,000 be made for the Mid-Northside Expanded Mental Health Services Program for the 2027 levy year?"
Background

The campaign estimates the 0.025% tax at about $4 for every $1,000 a property owner now pays in property tax. On its chart, a $4,000 tax bill rises $16 a year, a $6,000 bill $24, and an $8,000 bill $32. This research found no independent estimate.

On the ballot by: Petition of area residents, filed with the Chicago Board of Elections together with the program question.

Supporters
  • Coalition to Save Our Mental Health Centers (campaigns for a yes vote)
  • The Community Action Team of local residents that gathered the signatures
Opponents and critics
  • None named in the sources found.
Official and reference pages
  • Official candidate and referenda list, Chicago Board of Elections (Oct. 27, 2026)
  • Campaign voter guide, page 2, with the cost chart (Coalition to Save Our Mental Health Centers)
  • Campaign toolkit with service-area map (Coalition to Save Our Mental Health Centers)
Not verified (3)
  • The cost per homeowner comes only from the campaign's voter guide.
  • This research did not confirm what happens if only one of the two Mid-Northside questions passes.
  • The territory and the precinct check are the same as for the previous question.

Sources and method

  • Races and candidates: the Chicago Board of Elections candidate list, status of Oct. 27, 2026, 4:10 p.m. The Board marks it unofficial and updates it when filings change.
  • Districts: the Census Bureau geocoder (2026 legislative districts), the City of Chicago 2025 precinct map, and the Board's district precinct schedules.
  • School board subdistrict: precinct 46-23 splits between Subdistricts 2B and 4A. Public Act 103-0584 lists your census block (170310311002003) in Subdistrict 2B.
  • Endorsements: the Chicago Sun-Times makes no candidate endorsements. Chicago Tribune picks appear under "Race coverage" where the research found them.
  • Candidate summaries come from campaign sites, government pages, Ballotpedia, and news reports, each linked in its row. Facts that the research did not verify sit under "Not verified" in each row.
  • Bar ratings for judges: the Alliance of Bar Associations for Judicial Screening, the Chicago Bar Association, the Chicago Council of Lawyers, and Injustice Watch.
